findings.evidence: The published B page has no body text. The repository schema identifies the page body as its summary; add a concise summary of the examples page.

The statement quantifies over every group homomorphism f:G→H without restricting G and H to finite groups, while def-frattini-subgroup-of-a-finite-group defines Φ only for finite groups. The displayed inclusion is undefined for homomorphisms with an infinite source or target; restrict the statement and title to finite groups.

Both steps infer that a quotient is elementary abelian from abelianness and exponent at most p, but the local definition also requires a finite p-group. The proof does not establish that P/Φ(P) and P/N have p-power order. Show by coset counting or Lagrange that each quotient of P by a normal subgroup is finite of p-power order before applying the elementary-abelian definition.

The proof establishes that P/K is abelian of exponent p and immediately calls it elementary abelian. The local definition also requires P/K to be a finite p-group; establish this from K≤P and Lagrange, then apply the largest-elementary-quotient criterion.

The proof treats M/Φ(P) and intermediate subgroups of E as vector subspaces without establishing that subgroups of an elementary abelian p-group are closed under the canonical Fp scalar action. Add the one-line argument that a subgroup is closed under x↦x^a for every integer representative a.

The fixed-point corollary requires q not to divide the size of each Frattini coset. The proof says each coset has |Φ(P)| elements and this is a p-power by Lagrange, but it does not supply the coset bijection or the fact that a divisor of p^n is a p-power. Show the coset-size equality and use Lagrange plus prime-power divisibility before applying the fixed-point result.
The cited power-order result gives ord(g^p), not by itself |⟨g^p⟩|. The proof needs the order-characterization |⟨x⟩|=ord(x), then gcd(p,p^n)=p, to establish the claimed subgroup order.

The quotient P/Φ(P) is asserted to have order p, but the proof does not compute the index from |P|=p^n and |Φ(P)|=p^(n−1). Include the Lagrange or coset count, then verify that gΦ(P) is nonzero before calling it a one-vector basis.
The proof asserts every nonzero vector has order p without showing it. Verify coordinatewise that p kills every vector and that for 1≤k

Associativity is only asserted as a direct substitution, and the proposed inverse is not checked on either side. Show the coordinate associativity calculation and verify both products with (-a,-b,-c+ab), or explicitly use associativity of matrix multiplication via the displayed bijection.

The commutator formula (0,0,ab′−a′b) is stated as the result of a calculation, but no expansion using the inverse formula is supplied. Include the multiplication that derives it before concluding H′ is the central axis.

The formula (a,b,c)^m=(ma,mb,mc+binom(m,2)ab) is asserted by induction without a base case or successor computation. Give the recurrence for the third coordinate, then justify the odd-p and p=2 cases from that formula.
